deities: Tulja Bhavani (form of Goddess Durga/Kali; Swayambhu 3-ft granite idol with eight arms holding weapons and the head of Mahisha)
festivals: Navratri / Tuljapur Bhavani Festival (twice a year - Sharad and Chaitra Navratri)

history.dynasty: Yadava/Kadamba dynasty (temple elevated to prominence under the Yadavas); resurgence under the Marathas
history.period: Present temple dated to the 12th century (1169; built by Mahamandaleshwara Maradadeva of the Kadamba dynasty); Hemadpanthi architecture
history.summary: The Tulja Bhavani Temple at Tuljapur in Dharashiv district is one of the 51 Shakti Peethas and one of Maharashtra's three-and-a-half peethas. Legend: the goddess, called Tvarita ('the swift one', later Tulja), appeared on Yamunachala hill to save the devotee Anubhuti from the demon Kukur, and is believed to have slain Mahishasura here. The deity is Swayambhu (self-manifested) - a 3-ft black-granite, eight-armed idol - and a 'chala' (movable) deity, moved from her throne several times a year. She was the kuldevi of the Bhonsle clan; Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj visited before campaigns and legend says she gifted him the Bhavani Talwar. The temple survived Delhi Sultanate invasions; Afzal Khan is said to have damaged the idol, an act avenged at Pratapgad. It is managed by the Shri Tulja Bhavani Temple Trust headed by the District Collector.

name: Tulja Bhavani Temple
town_description: Tuljapur is a temple town in Dharashiv district (formerly Osmanabad) of Maharashtra, set on the Yamunachala ranges at about 2,150 ft elevation, roughly 45 km from Solapur. It takes its name from the Tulja Bhavani temple and draws lakhs of pilgrims yearly from Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, who also regard the goddess as kuldevi. The town's other shrines - Ghat Shila, Chintamani, Dhakte Bhavani - plus the nearby Naldurg fort and Dharashiv caves make it a combined pilgrimage and heritage stop; it comes alive with fairs during Navratri.

visitor_information.best_time: October to March (15-30C). Sharad Navratri (Sept-Oct) and Chaitra Navratri (Mar-Apr) are the grandest but most crowded; early morning (6-9 AM) or evening for calmer darshan.

Temple open nearly round the clock during Navratri. Entry is free; VIP/special darshan passes bookable at shrituljabhavani.org (verify).
